events.title: Croton destroys Sybaris
events.summary: Croton, led in the field by the Olympic wrestler Milo, routed the army of Sybaris at the river Traeis and then razed the richest Greek city in Italy, reportedly diverting the Crathis over its ruins.
events.detail: The quarrel began when the Sybarite tyrant Telys drove 500 rich citizens into exile and Croton, persuaded by Pythagoras, refused to surrender them. Diodorus' figures of 300,000 Sybarites against 100,000 Crotoniates are fantasies, but the outcome was real: Sybaris' coinage ends abruptly, Croton became the leading power of the Ionian coast, and the survivors' attempts to refound the city culminated in the pan-Hellenic colony of Thurii (444/443). Herodotus heard a Sybarite version in which Dorieus of Sparta helped Croton, which the Crotoniates denied. The fall of Sybaris is the backdrop to Pythagorean political dominance in Croton and to the later anti-Pythagorean revolts.

battle.significance: Removed the dominant city of Magna Graecia and redistributed power along the Ionian coast.

events.debate: Ancient numbers are absurd; whether the river was really diverted is doubted, but excavation at Sibari shows heavy alluviation over the archaic city.

events.title: Royalist conspiracy and the execution of Brutus' sons
events.summary: Envoys of the exiled Tarquins, sent to reclaim the royal property, recruited young nobles of the Vitellii and Aquilii, among them Titus and Tiberius, sons of the consul Brutus; a slave, Vindicius, betrayed the plot and Brutus watched his own sons scourged and beheaded.
events.detail: The story is the founding exemplum of Republican severitas: the consul's duty to the state overrides the father's love. The plotters met in the house of the Aquilii, nephews of Collatinus, and wrote letters to Tarquin that were seized. Vindicius was rewarded with freedom and citizenship, and later Romans derived the word vindicta (the rod used in manumission) from his name, an obvious aetiology. The Senate first voted to return the Tarquins' goods, then, after the plot, gave them to the plebs to plunder. Livy places the trial on the consuls' tribunal; Dionysius gives a much longer set-piece with Collatinus pleading for his nephews, which helps explain his fall. Modern scholars treat the episode as legend built round the Junii Bruti, though plotting by exiled kings is entirely plausible.
events.debate: Vindicius and the vindicta are an aetiological invention; the Junii Bruti of the later Republic were plebeian, which raised doubts already in antiquity about descent from the patrician first consul.

events.title: Creation of the rex sacrorum
events.summary: To perform the sacrifices that only a king could offer, the Republic created a 'king of sacred things' (rex sacrorum or sacrificulus), first held by Manius Papirius, and made him subordinate to the pontifex maximus so that the title could never again carry power.
events.detail: The rex sacrorum, with his wife the regina, kept archaic duties: on the Kalends he announced the dates of the month, and after the Regifugium of 24 February he performed a sacrifice in the Comitium and fled. He was barred from all magistracies and from addressing the people. The survival of the office, attested down to the 4th century AD, is one of the strongest arguments that the monarchy really did end, and that its religious functions were split off rather than abolished. Some scholars argue that the king's sacral powers passed in stages, with the rex sacrorum dating from the early Republic but the pontifical supremacy over him developing later.

events.title: Collatinus forced into exile
events.summary: Because he bore the hated name Tarquinius, the consul L. Tarquinius Collatinus, Lucretia's husband, was persuaded by Brutus to resign; he withdrew to Lavinium with his property and a law of Brutus exiled the whole Tarquin gens.
events.detail: Livy makes Brutus plead with his colleague in a public assembly, and Collatinus' father-in-law Sp. Lucretius add his entreaty; Collatinus took 20 talents from Brutus as a gift (Livy) and went into exile. P. Valerius was elected in his place. The episode shows the tradition grappling with the fact that a Tarquin stood in the first consular college, and may reflect a real purge of the royal clan.

events.title: The Tarquins' field becomes the Campus Martius
events.summary: The royal estate between the city and the Tiber was consecrated to Mars; the grain standing on it, sacrilegious to eat, was thrown into the river, where it lodged in the shallows and, according to the legend, formed the Tiber Island.
events.detail: Livy, Dionysius and Plutarch tell the same aetiology. Geologically the island is a volcanic tufa outcrop, far older than Rome, but the story records a genuine memory that the Campus Martius had once been crown land. The Campus became the mustering ground of the centuriate assembly and the site of the censors' lustrum; the island later received the cult of Aesculapius (291), which is why it was faced in travertine as a ship.
events.debate: The island story is pure aetiology; whether the Campus was really royal property is uncertain.

events.title: Valerius demolishes his house on the Velia
events.summary: When rumours spread that P. Valerius, sole consul after Brutus' death, was building a fortress-house on the Velia to make himself king, he had it pulled down in a single night, rebuilt below the hill, and lowered his fasces before the assembly; hence the name Publicola, 'friend of the people'.
events.detail: The episode is the origin legend for two conventions: magistrates' fasces were lowered (fasces summittere) before the sovereign people, and the axes were removed from the fasces inside the city, since there a citizen could appeal (provocatio). It is tied to the lex Valeria de provocatione, the first of three such laws attributed to the Valerii (509, 449, 300), and almost certainly reflects Valerian family propaganda transmitted by the annalist Valerius Antias.

events.title: Treasury placed under the quaestors
events.summary: Plutarch credits Publicola with making the Temple of Saturn the state treasury (aerarium Saturni) and letting the people elect two quaestors to manage it, the first being P. Veturius and M. Minucius.
events.detail: The attribution is anachronistic: the Temple of Saturn was dedicated only in 498 or 497, and Tacitus believed quaestors already existed under the kings, chosen by them, and were first elected in 447. What is not in doubt is the long association of the quaestors with the aerarium in the podium of the temple, where state funds, the military standards and copies of laws and senatus consulta were kept.
events.debate: Origins of the quaestorship disputed: royal appointees, consular assistants chosen from 509, or elected from 447.

events.title: Census of 508: 130,000 citizens
events.summary: Dionysius records a census of 130,000 adult male citizens in the consulship of Valerius and Lucretius, the first of a series of early figures that grow implausibly large.
events.detail: Rome's territory around 500 was about 820 km2 (Beloch's estimate), able to feed perhaps 25,000-40,000 people in all. The early census totals in Dionysius and Livy are thus best read as later reconstructions, or as including women and children, or as projections back from 3rd-century figures. They matter because Roman antiquarians believed them and used them to describe the Republic's growth.
scholarship: Beloch, Die Bevölkerung der griechisch-römischen Welt (1886)
events.debate: Totals are unreliable; Brunt and others reject all census figures before the 4th century.

events.title: Sabine war and the first ovation
events.summary: In 505 the consuls M. Valerius Volusus and P. Postumius Tubertus defeated the Sabines; fighting resumed in 504 (Publicola's last triumph) and 503, when Postumius Tubertus entered the city 'ovans', the first recorded ovation, crowned with myrtle rather than laurel.
events.detail: Livy reports the Sabine victories briefly; the war is notable for its ritual firsts. Pliny says Postumius Tubertus was the first to celebrate an ovation, wearing a crown of myrtle sacred to Venus Victrix, because he had won 'without bloodshed'. The Fasti Triumphales list triumphs of M. Valerius (505) and P. Valerius (504) over the Sabines. The secession of Attus Clausus and his clients to Rome in 504 was a by-product of Sabine divisions over the war.

events.title: Death and public funeral of Publicola
events.summary: P. Valerius Publicola, four times consul, died so poor that he was buried at public expense, and the matrons mourned him for a year as they had Brutus; his descendants kept the rare right of burial inside the city at the foot of the Velia.
events.detail: Plutarch reports that the Valerii marked the right by setting a torch under a body at the family site and then removing it, a symbolic claim rather than a real burial. The poverty motif recurs in Menenius Agrippa (493) and Cincinnatus, and expresses a later ideal of early Roman frugality.

events.title: Siege and destruction of Suessa Pometia
events.summary: The Latin colonies of Pometia and Cora went over to the Aurunci in 503; after a sortie burned the Roman siege works and wounded a consul, Pometia was taken in 502, its leaders beheaded, the population sold and the town razed.
events.detail: Livy admits that his sources confused this siege with others, and the Fasti Triumphales record a triumph over the Aurunci in 503. Suessa Pometia had been rich enough for Tarquinius Superbus to fund the Capitoline temple from its booty (40 talents according to Fabius Pictor, 400 per Piso). The site has never been located with certainty; candidates lie around Cisterna and Latina, near Satricum.

battle.significance: Removed a Volscian-Auruncan foothold on the edge of the Alban hills; the episode illustrates the instability of the Pontine borderland.

events.debate: Location unknown; Livy himself suspects duplication with the capture of Pometia under Tarquin and in 495.

events.title: Pre-monetary bronze: aes rude and the libral as
events.summary: For two centuries after 509 Rome had no coins: payments, fines and dowries were made in bronze weighed on a balance (aes rude, shapeless lumps), reckoned in asses of a Roman pound, while older fines were expressed in sheep and oxen.
events.detail: Timaeus, quoted by Pliny, knew that the Romans used aes rude before any coin, and Pliny credited Servius Tullius with first 'marking' bronze. The Twelve Tables fix penalties in asses (25 for an iniuria, 300 for breaking a free man's bone) and the lex Aternia Tarpeia (454) converted livestock fines at one ox = 100 asses and one sheep = 10. Transactions by bronze and scales (per aes et libram) survived as ritual in mancipatio and nexum, with a libripens holding the balance. Fragments of aes rude occur in votive deposits across central Italy (at sanctuaries such as Lavinium and Vicarello) and continue in hoards alongside aes grave into the 3rd century. Words such as aestimare, stipendium (from stips, small bronze) and expendere preserve the system.
scholarship: Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987)

events.title: Aes signatum 'ramo secco' currency bars
events.summary: Cast bronze bars marked with a 'dry branch' (ramo secco) or fishbone pattern circulated in Etruria, Emilia and Umbria between the 6th and 4th centuries, usually broken into fragments and weighed; they are Etruscan, not Roman, the ancestors of the later Roman aes signatum.
events.detail: Ramo secco bars typically weigh 1-2 kg when whole and are found mostly as fragments in hoards and votive deposits, showing that value lay in weight, not in the mark. Their distribution from the Po valley to Latium shows that central Italy shared a bronze-weight economy long before coinage, which explains why Roman cast coinage of c. 280 began at such a heavy standard.
scholarship: Crawford, Coinage and Money under the Roman Republic (1985)
Burnett, Coinage in the Roman World (1987)

events.title: Latin dedication of the grove of Diana at Aricia
events.summary: Cato recorded that Egerius Baevius of Tusculum, as dictator Latinus, dedicated the grove of Diana at Aricia on behalf of Tusculum, Aricia, Lanuvium, Laurentum, Cora, Tibur, Pometia and Ardea; Rome is not on the list.
events.detail: The fragment, preserved by Priscian, is the clearest evidence for a Latin federal cult and for a common Latin chief magistrate. Many scholars date it to c. 500, after the expulsion of the Tarquins, when the Latins under Tusculan and Arician leadership organized against Rome; others place it in the 6th century as a rival to the Servian Diana cult on the Aventine. The sanctuary on Lake Nemi, with its rex Nemorensis who held office by killing his predecessor, became famous through Frazer's Golden Bough.
events.debate: Date (6th century or c. 500) and whether the list represents an anti-Roman league are disputed.

events.title: Commercial treaties between Carthage and the Etruscans
events.summary: Aristotle cites the Etruscans and Carthaginians as peoples bound by agreements on imports, conventions against wrongdoing and written alliances, yet not forming one state; the Pyrgi tablets and the joint fleet at Alalia confirm a long Etrusco-Punic partnership.
events.detail: The partnership shaped Rome's world. The first Roman treaty with Carthage (509) belongs to the same family of agreements, regulating trade and protecting coastal Latin cities. The Pyrgi gold tablets, in Etruscan and Phoenician, show the ruler of Caere honouring Astarte (Uni) around 500. The alliance ended with Etruscan sea power after Cumae (474) and Syracusan raids (453, 384).

events.title: Crustumerium taken; Praeneste joins Rome
events.summary: In 499 Rome besieged Fidenae and captured Crustumerium, a Latin town on the Via Salaria, while Praeneste broke with the Latins and went over to Rome, on the eve of the war that ended at Lake Regillus.
events.detail: Crustumerium's territory became the Clustumina tribe, the only early rustic tribe named after a place rather than a gens. Excavated cemeteries show the town was largely abandoned in the early 5th century, matching the tradition.

events.title: Census under the first dictator: 150,700
events.summary: Dionysius says the first dictator, T. Larcius, held a census which found 150,700 men of military age; Livy dates Larcius' dictatorship to 501.
events.detail: The figure fits the pattern of inflated early census totals (130,000 in 508, 110,000 in 493, 103,000 in 474) and was probably derived by later antiquarians from family archives or invented.
events.debate: Chronology of the first dictatorship (501 Livy, 498 Dionysius) and the census total are both suspect.

events.title: Twenty-one tribes
events.summary: Livy notes under 495 that 'twenty-one tribes were made at Rome': four urban tribes inherited from Servius Tullius and seventeen rustic tribes, most named after patrician gentes, plus the Clustumina; the number did not rise again until 387.
events.detail: The rustic tribes bearing gentile names (Aemilia, Camilia, Claudia, Cornelia, Fabia, Galeria, Horatia, Lemonia, Menenia, Papiria, Pollia, Pupinia, Romilia, Sergia, Voltinia, Voturia) suggest districts where those clans held land, a striking picture of aristocratic territorial power in the early Republic. The Claudia was tied to the arrival of Attus Clausus in 504. The tribe was a unit for the census, levy and tributum, and from 471 for the plebeian assembly. The sixteen gentile tribes all lay within about 8-10 km of Rome, mapping the ager Romanus antiquus. Taylor's reconstruction of tribal geography remains standard.
scholarship: L. R. Taylor, The Voting Districts of the Roman Republic (1960)
events.debate: Whether 21 includes the Clustumina, and whether Dionysius' figure (21 in 491) reflects the same reform; the origins of gentile-named tribes are debated.

events.title: Volscian and Auruncan war of 495
events.summary: With the plebs refusing the levy, the consul P. Servilius won recruits by an edict protecting debtors' property while they served, defeated the Volsci and sacked Suessa Pometia, and then routed an Auruncan army near Aricia.
events.detail: Livy uses the campaign to dramatise the debt crisis: the soldiers who had won the war returned to find Appius Claudius enforcing debt judgments, leading to the secession of 494. The Fasti record no triumph for Servilius, whom the Senate refused one; Livy says he triumphed by popular decision, perhaps a retrojection of later practice.

battle.significance: Cleared the Alban approaches; set the stage for the debt crisis of 494.

events.title: The old centurion and the debt riots of 495
events.summary: An aged former centurion, his farm burned in the Sabine war and himself enslaved for debt, burst into the Forum showing battle scars on his chest and the marks of the lash on his back; the crowd rioted and the plebs refused to serve.
events.detail: Livy's scene is a literary set-piece, but it captures the mechanism of nexum: a citizen who could not repay pledged his own labour and person, and the creditor could chain and beat him. The consul Appius Claudius enforced debt judgments harshly, his colleague Servilius promised relief, and the Senate's failure to legislate produced the First Secession the following year.

events.title: Dictatorship of Manius Valerius (494)
events.summary: Facing Sabine, Aequian and Volscian attacks and a plebs that would not enlist, the Senate named the popular Manius Valerius dictator; he raised ten legions, triumphed over the Sabines, but resigned when the Senate refused the debt relief he had promised the soldiers.
events.detail: The dictator's edict suspended debt actions during the war, the device that made the levy possible. His resignation rather than a betrayal of his pledge earned him plebeian gratitude; the soldiers, still under oath, marched out and seceded to the Mons Sacer. Livy's 'ten legions' is an anachronism of the 'legion' as a later unit; the early army was a single legio of perhaps 3,000-6,000.
events.debate: Some sources (DH) make Manius Valerius brother of Publicola; the scale of the levy is anachronistic.

events.title: Colonists sent to Velitrae
events.summary: Velitrae, a Volscian town on the southern slopes of the Alban hills, was taken in 494 and received Roman colonists, reinforced in 492 after plague emptied it; it repeatedly revolted and was harshly punished in 338.
events.detail: Velitrae was the home town of the Octavii, Augustus' paternal family. The Tabula Veliterna, a Volscian inscription of the 3rd century, shows that Volscian speech survived there long after colonisation.

events.title: Plebeian aediles created
events.summary: Alongside the first tribunes the plebs elected two aediles, assistants of the tribunes based at the Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera, who kept the plebeian archives and later the copies of senatus consulta.
events.detail: The name derives from aedes, the temple. The aediles policed markets and grain supply, administered fines collected by the plebs, and organised the plebeian games. From 449 copies of decrees were deposited with them at the Ceres temple to prevent consular tampering. The temple of the Aventine triad thus acted as a plebeian counter-Capitol, with its own treasury and archive.
events.locName: Temple of Ceres, near the Aventine

events.title: Census of 493: 110,000
events.summary: After the Foedus Cassianum Dionysius records a census of slightly over 110,000 citizens.
events.detail: The drop from his figure of 150,700 for 498 may reflect a tradition of losses in the Latin war and the secession, or simply inconsistent invented numbers.

events.title: Lex Icilia protecting tribunes' speech
events.summary: Dionysius reports a law carried by the tribune Sp. Icilius forbidding anyone to interrupt or contradict a tribune addressing the plebs, on pain of a fine or death.
events.detail: The law, if genuine, protected the tribune's ius agendi cum plebe, the right to convene and address the plebs, which became the basis of plebeian legislation. It fits a cluster of early laws in which the plebs, as a sworn community, protected their officers by a lex sacrata.
events.debate: Known only from Dionysius; its authenticity is doubtful.

events.title: Trial and exile of Coriolanus
events.summary: When grain sent from Sicily arrived during the famine, Cn. Marcius Coriolanus urged the Senate to sell it dear unless the plebs gave up the tribunate; the tribunes indicted him, he refused to appear, was condemned in absence and fled to the Volsci.
events.detail: Livy names the donor vaguely as a Sicilian tyrant; Dionysius makes it Gelon, whereas other annalists named Dionysius I, an anachronism Dionysius himself pointed out. Dionysius presents the trial as the first before an assembly voting by tribes, a procedure scholars think he retrojected from the 4th century. Coriolanus went to Antium and to Attius Tullius, chief of the Volsci, with whom he planned the war of 488. The legend of a patrician war hero turned traitor through hatred of the plebs became a model in Plutarch and Shakespeare; modern scholars suspect a Volscian war leader called Marcius was fused with a Roman aristocratic myth.
events.debate: Historicity of Coriolanus and of a tribal trial in 491 is widely doubted; the grain donor's identity was already contested in antiquity.

events.title: The Roman Games repeated after Titus Latinius' dream
events.summary: A master had a slave flogged through the Circus before the procession of the Ludi Romani; Jupiter told the farmer T. Latinius in a dream that the 'leading dancer' displeased him; when Latinius delayed, his son died and he was paralysed, until he told the Senate and walked home cured, and the games were held again.
events.detail: The episode is the classic example of instauratio: any ritual flaw required the whole ceremony to be repeated. Cicero cites it from Fabius Pictor, which makes it one of the oldest recorded stories of Roman religion. Livy places it on the eve of Coriolanus' war; Macrobius used it to explain the festival called the 'Day of the Slave'.

events.title: Assassination of Aristodemus of Cumae
events.summary: Aristodemus 'the Effeminate', tyrant of Cumae and host of the exiled Tarquinius Superbus, was murdered by the sons of the aristocrats he had killed, ending the tyranny some years after Tarquin's death.
events.detail: Dionysius gives a long, partly romantic narrative based on a Cumaean chronicle, which is also an important independent source for the battle of Aricia (504). Aristodemus confiscated the Roman grain ships of 492 as compensation for Tarquin's property. Plutarch preserves a story that the courtesan Xenocrite helped the plotters.
events.debate: Date uncertain, c. 490-480.

events.title: Anaxilas of Rhegium seizes Zancle and renames it Messana
events.summary: Anaxilas, tyrant of Rhegium (c. 494-476), encouraged Samian and Milesian refugees from the Ionian revolt to seize Zancle, then expelled them and resettled the city, renaming it Messana after his family's Messenian origin; for a generation he controlled both sides of the Strait.
events.detail: Anaxilas married his daughter to Hiero of Syracuse but was the father-in-law and ally of Terillus of Himera, whose appeal brought the Carthaginian invasion of 480. His coinage at Rhegium and Messana shows a hare and a mule-car, commemorating an Olympic victory with mules. The control of the Strait recurs in Roman history: the Mamertines' seizure of Messana in 288 and their appeal of 264 began the First Punic War.
events.debate: Chronology of the Samian seizure (c. 494-493) and the renaming (c. 488 or later) is disputed.

events.title: Temple of Fortuna Muliebris
events.summary: Where Veturia, Volumnia and the matrons turned back Coriolanus, the Senate founded a shrine of Women's Fortune, whose first priestess was Valeria; its statue was said to have spoken, and only women married once (univirae) could touch it.
events.detail: Dionysius gives a detailed foundation narrative: the Senate offered the women a reward, they asked for a temple, and it was dedicated at public expense with a second statue paid for by the matrons. The cult and its location at the boundary of the early ager Romanus are real; the connection to Coriolanus is aetiology. The temple was restored under Augustus by Livia. It is one of a cluster of women's cults (Mater Matuta, Pudicitia, Venus Verticordia) whose foundation legends served as exempla of matronly virtue.
events.locName: Fourth milestone of the Via Latina
events.debate: Dates of vow (488) and dedication (487 or 486) vary in the sources.

events.title: Gelon makes Syracuse his capital
events.summary: Gelon, tyrant of Gela, intervened when the Syracusan landowners (gamoroi) were expelled by the demos and their serfs; he took the city, left Gela to his brother Hiero, and turned Syracuse into the greatest city of the Greek West by transplanting the populations of Camarina, Gela and Megara Hyblaea.
events.detail: Herodotus describes the deportations in detail: the rich of Megara were made citizens, the common people sold abroad. Gelon could field 20,000 hoplites and 200 triremes when the Greek allies asked his help against Xerxes in 481, and he refused unless given command. The resources concentrated at Syracuse explain the victory at Himera (480), and the city's later role as Rome's partner and rival.

events.title: Seven years of Fabian consuls
events.summary: From 485 to 479 a Fabius held one of the two consulships every year: Quintus (485, 482), Caeso (484, 481, 479) and Marcus (483, 480), an aristocratic dominance unparalleled in the Fasti, ended by the clan's private war against Veii.
events.detail: The Fabii first appear as hard-line opponents of Sp. Cassius' agrarian law (Caeso as quaestor prosecuted Cassius in 485, according to one version), then switch to conciliating the plebs: Caeso proposed in 479 that conquered land be distributed. Livy explains the Cremera expedition as the gens offering to fight Veii at its own cost. The run of consulships may be genuine, reflecting a gens with its own tribe (Fabia) and huge clientela, or partly the work of Fabius Pictor, Rome's first historian, glorifying his family.
events.debate: Possible family embellishment by Fabius Pictor.

events.title: Execution of the Vestal Oppia
events.summary: Amid prodigies and war with Veii and the Volsci, the soothsayers declared that rites were being improperly performed; the Vestal Oppia (Opimia in Dionysius) was convicted of unchastity and put to death.
events.detail: Vestals convicted of incestum were buried alive in an underground chamber at the Campus Sceleratus by the Colline Gate, so that no one shed their blood. The early cases (Oppia 483, Urbinia 472, Postumia accused 420, Minucia 337, Sextilia 273) cluster in years of crisis, showing that Vestal chastity was felt as the city's safety.

events.title: Theron builds the Olympieion of Acragas with Carthaginian prisoners
events.summary: After Himera Theron of Acragas set thousands of Carthaginian prisoners to work on public projects: the vast Temple of Olympian Zeus, c. 113 by 56 m with giant telamon figures, the city's drains (named phaeaces after their architect Phaeax) and an artificial fishpond.
events.detail: Diodorus says some private Acragantines owned 500 prisoners each. The Olympieion, the largest Doric temple ever begun, was left unroofed when the Carthaginians sacked the city in 406; one reconstructed telamon is 7.6 m tall. The prisoners also built the temple at Himera. The scale of the programme illustrates how much wealth the defeat of Carthage transferred to the Sicilian tyrants.

events.title: Peace terms after Himera and the Damareteion
events.summary: After Himera Carthage obtained peace from Gelon for 2,000 talents of silver and the building of two temples where copies of the treaty would be kept; Gelon's wife Damarete, who had interceded for the Carthaginians, received a gold crown of 100 talents.
events.detail: Diodorus says Damarete coined silver from the crown, the 'Damareteion' worth ten Attic drachmas, which numismatists long identified with the magnificent Syracusan decadrachms showing Arethusa and a lion; modern die studies date those coins to the 460s, after the fall of the Deinomenids. The peace held for seventy years, until Carthage returned in 409.
events.debate: Identification and date of the Damareteion decadrachm disputed (c. 479 or c. 465).

events.title: Battle before Veii and the soldiers' oath (480)
events.summary: Soldiers who had refused to win victories for unpopular consuls were stung by Etruscan taunts and swore an oath, led by the centurion M. Flavoleius, to return victorious; Rome won, but the former consul Q. Fabius and the consul Cn. Manlius were killed and M. Fabius declined the triumph.
events.detail: Veii was supported by contingents from all Etruria, according to Livy. Fabius' refusal to triumph in a year of public mourning, and his care of the wounded in patrician houses, are presented as the turning point that reconciled the Fabii with the plebs, leading to the clan's volunteer war at the Cremera. The battle cost Rome heavily; the war continued until the forty-year truce of 474.

sides.losses: heavy; a consul and an ex-consul killed

battle.significance: Costly victory; prelude to the Fabian expedition and the Cremera disaster.

events.title: Hiero I refounds Catana as Aetna
events.summary: Hiero expelled the citizens of Catana and Naxos and settled 10,000 new colonists (half Syracusans, half Peloponnesians) at Catana, renamed Aetna, with his son Deinomenes as its king; Pindar's First Pythian and Aeschylus' 'Women of Aetna' celebrated the foundation.
events.detail: Hiero wanted to be honoured as a founder (oikistes) with hero cult after death, and was. After the Deinomenid fall the original Catanians returned (461) and the Aetnaeans moved to Inessa, renamed Aetna.

events.title: Veientes occupy the Janiculum
events.summary: Exploiting the Cremera disaster, the Veientes seized the Janiculum and crossed the Tiber; after fights at the Temple of Spes and the Colline Gate they were dislodged in 476, though the consul Sp. Servilius nearly lost his army attacking the hill.
events.detail: The occupation caused a grain shortage in Rome. The fighting shows how close the Veientine frontier lay: the right bank of the Tiber (ripa Veiens) was Etruscan territory, and control of the salt road and Tiber crossings was the issue in the Veientine wars.

battle.significance: Restored Rome's hold on the Tiber crossing.

events.title: Trial of Titus Menenius for the Cremera
events.summary: The tribunes Q. Considius and T. Genucius prosecuted the consul of 477, T. Menenius, son of Agrippa, for failing to relieve the Fabii at the Cremera; he was fined 2,000 asses and died soon after; in 475 Sp. Servilius was acquitted on a similar charge.
events.detail: These are the first tribunician prosecutions of ex-consuls in Livy, a weapon of plebeian pressure that became regular. The 2,000-asses fine is expressed in bronze by weight, since Rome had no coins.

events.title: Census of 474: 103,000
events.summary: Dionysius gives slightly over 103,000 citizens at the lustrum of 474, the year of the forty-year truce with Veii.
events.detail: Lower than his earlier figures, the total may preserve a tradition of losses in the Veientine war.

events.title: Iapygians annihilate the Tarentines and Rhegines
events.summary: The Iapygians (Messapians) inflicted on Tarentum and its Rhegine allies what Herodotus called the greatest slaughter of Greeks he knew; 3,000 Rhegines fell, and the losses among the Tarentine nobility led to a democratic constitution at Tarentum.
events.detail: Diodorus adds that the Iapygians pursued the Rhegines to Rhegium itself. Aristotle cites the defeat as a case where loss of the notables changed a constitution. Tarentum recovered and, with new dedications at Delphi from Messapian spoils, became the dominant Italiote power of the 4th century.

battle.significance: Worst Greek defeat in Italy before the 4th century; produced the Tarentine democracy.

events.title: Murder of the tribune Gnaeus Genucius
events.summary: The tribune Cn. Genucius indicted the consuls of 474 for not appointing the agrarian commission; on the morning of the trial he was found dead in his house, and the frightened tribunes dropped the case, while the consuls pressed the levy.
events.detail: Livy implies patrician murder without proof. The episode led directly to Volero Publilius' defiance of the levy and to the lex Publilia of 471 transferring tribunician elections to an assembly by tribes. It shows sacrosanctity as a sworn plebeian protection that did not stop secret violence.

events.title: The Vestal Urbinia buried alive
events.summary: During a plague that struck women and unborn children, the Vestal Urbinia was convicted of unchastity and buried alive; one of her lovers killed himself and the other was scourged in the Forum and executed.
events.detail: Dionysius is the only source. The double punishment of Vestal and seducer became standard. The Campus Sceleratus lay inside the Colline Gate near the later Baths of Diocletian.
events.locName: Campus Sceleratus, by the Colline Gate

events.title: Trial and death of Appius Claudius (cos. 471)
events.summary: Appius Claudius, the consul of 471 who had fought the lex Publilia and decimated his army, was prosecuted by the tribunes M. Duillius and Cn. Siccius for obstructing the agrarian law; he died before judgement, by illness or suicide, and his son delivered his funeral eulogy over tribunician protests.
events.detail: Livy's Claudii are consistently arrogant patricians, a stereotype that Mommsen and later Wiseman traced to hostile annalists, notably Licinius Macer. The case belongs to the run of tribunician prosecutions of the 470s.
events.debate: The Claudian stereotype in Livy is likely literary.

events.title: Tomb of the Diver at Poseidonia
events.summary: A cist tomb of c. 480-470 found in 1968 near Poseidonia bears the only surviving Greek figured wall painting of its date: symposiasts on the walls and, on the lid, a young man diving from a platform into water.
events.detail: The diver is usually read as a metaphor for the passage from life to death. Poseidonia was still Greek; around 410 the Lucanians took the city, and the painted tombs of the Lucanian period (4th century) show armoured horsemen and women mourners in Oscan dress.
scholarship: M. Napoli, La Tomba del Tuffatore (1970)

events.title: T. Quinctius takes Antium
events.summary: The consul T. Quinctius Capitolinus defeated the Volsci and captured Antium, their chief port, in 468; the city was colonised the next year but soon reverted to Volscian control.
events.detail: Antium alternated between Roman and Volscian hands until its final capture in 338, when the beaks of its ships were fixed to the speakers' platform in the Forum.

battle.significance: Gave Rome a temporary foothold on the Volscian coast.

events.title: Colony at Antium (467)
events.summary: To deflect agrarian agitation the Senate sent a colony to Antium under three commissioners (T. Quinctius, A. Verginius, P. Furius); so few Romans enrolled that Volscians were admitted to fill the lists.
events.detail: Livy presents the colony as a patrician alternative to distributing public land near Rome. The mixed settlement shows that early 'Latin' colonies were federal and multi-ethnic, and help explain why Antium could revert to the Volsci.

events.title: Fall of the Deinomenid tyranny at Syracuse
events.summary: Thrasybulus, who succeeded his brother Hiero I in 467, was expelled within a year by a general rising; Syracuse became a democracy, instituting a festival of Zeus Eleutherios, and the tyrannies at Acragas and elsewhere also collapsed.
events.detail: The new democracy faced civil strife with Gelon's enfranchised mercenaries, who were finally expelled. It experimented with petalism, an ostracism by olive leaves (454). Syracusan democracy lasted until Dionysius I seized power in 405, and fought off the Athenian expedition of 415-413.

events.title: Dedication of the Temple of Semo Sancus Dius Fidius
events.summary: The temple of the oath-god Semo Sancus Dius Fidius on the Quirinal, begun by the Tarquins, was dedicated by Sp. Postumius on 5 June 466; it held the archaic treaty with Gabii written on an ox-hide shield.
events.detail: Dionysius saw the Gabine treaty there. The temple also held a bronze statue of Gaia Caecilia (Tanaquil) with her distaff and spindle, and Varro said oaths 'me Dius Fidius' were sworn under its open roof. A base inscribed to Semo Sancus found on the Tiber Island led Justin Martyr to think Romans worshipped Simon Magus.

events.title: Terentilius Harsa demands written limits on consular power
events.summary: The tribune C. Terentilius Harsa proposed a five-man commission to write down the limits of consular imperium, so that consuls could no longer use their power as they pleased; patrician resistance kept the bill blocked for nearly a decade, until the plebs won the decemvirate of 451.
events.detail: Livy portrays Terentilius' rogation as the opening of the campaign that produced the Twelve Tables: an attack on the arbitrary coercive power (coercitio) of patrician magistrates and on the secrecy of law held by the pontiffs. Year after year the same tribunes were re-elected to push it, and the patricians answered with levies, violence by young nobles such as Caeso Quinctius, and religious obstruction. By 454 the plebs had shifted to demanding a general codification for both orders, which the patricians accepted on condition that the codifiers be patricians. The details are annalistic reconstruction, but a long agitation for written law preceding 451 is plausible and mirrors developments in the Greek world.
events.debate: The repeated tribunician colleges and the pattern of annual agitation are probably annalistic elaboration.

events.title: Trial of Caeso Quinctius and the first sureties
events.summary: Caeso Quinctius, son of Cincinnatus and leader of the young patricians who drove tribunes from the Forum, was accused on capital charges; ten sureties (vades) pledged 3,000 asses each for his appearance, the first such bail recorded at Rome, but he fled to Etruria and his father sold his estate to pay.
events.detail: The key witness, the former tribune M. Volscius Fictor, said Caeso had beaten his brother so badly that he died; in 459 Volscius was convicted of perjury and exiled. The impoverishment of Cincinnatus, reduced to four iugera beyond the Tiber, sets up the famous plough scene of 458. Livy uses Caeso to show patrician youth violence as a political weapon against the tribunate.

events.title: Rain of flesh
events.summary: Among the prodigies of 461 Livy records that flesh rained from the sky, birds snatching pieces in mid-air and the rest lying on the ground for days without rotting; the Sibylline Books were consulted.
events.detail: The Books warned of danger from foreigners gathering in the city and urged avoidance of sedition, an answer the patricians used against the tribunes. The episode is an early example of the prodigy-and-expiation cycle that structured Roman religious life.

events.title: Ducetius and the Sicel league
events.summary: The Sicel leader Ducetius united the native towns of eastern Sicily into a league, founded new cities at Menaenum and Palike, and fought Syracuse and Acragas; defeated in 450, he threw himself as a suppliant on the altars of Syracuse, was exiled to Corinth, returned to found Kale Akte, and died in 440.
events.detail: Ducetius' movement is the one serious attempt by an indigenous Sicilian people to build a state against the Greek cities. He exploited the turmoil after the fall of the Deinomenids, sited his federal capital beside the sacred lake of the Palici (the twin gods of oaths), and in 451 took the Acragantine fort of Motyon. Syracuse spared him, which caused a war with Acragas. Diodorus, drawing on Timaeus, is the only narrative source; excavations at Rocchicella di Mineo have found the sanctuary.
events.locName: Palike, near the sanctuary of the Palici

events.title: Syracusan fleet raids Etruria, Elba and Corsica
events.summary: Syracuse sent the admiral Phayllus against 'Tyrrhenian pirates'; when he took bribes and was exiled, Apelles followed with 60 triremes, ravaged the Etruscan coast and Corsica, seized Elba and returned with many captives.
events.detail: Elba (Aethalia) was the source of Etruscan iron, smelted at Populonia. The raids continued the Syracusan offensive begun at Cumae in 474 and weakened Etruscan sea power at the moment when Rome was consolidating against Veii. Dionysius I repeated the exercise with the sack of Pyrgi in 384.

battle.significance: Further reduced Etruscan control of the Tyrrhenian Sea.

events.title: Plague of 453
events.summary: A pestilence killed the consul Sex. Quinctilius, the flamen Quirinalis Ser. Cornelius and the augur C. Horatius Pulvillus, and many of the poor; the codification debate paused while the embassy to Greece was away.
events.detail: Livy's notice comes from priestly lists, which recorded deaths in the colleges, and is therefore one of the more credible early items.

events.title: The Second Decemvirate
events.summary: Appius Claudius had himself re-elected with nine new colleagues, including several of plebeian name; the board added two tables, among them the ban on intermarriage between patricians and plebeians, and then refused to lay down office when its year ended.
events.detail: Livy contrasts the moderate first board with a second that appeared with 120 lictors, all carrying axes, and ruled by terror. Cicero called the conubium ban 'most inhuman'. The plebeian names in the college (Poetelius, Duillius, Rabuleius, Oppius, Antonius) have led modern scholars to suspect that the tyranny story distorts a genuinely mixed board, and that the conubium clause was itself a codification of existing patrician exclusivity. The decemvirate fell in 449 after the Verginia affair and the Second Secession.
events.debate: Whether plebeians sat on the second board, and whether the tyranny narrative is a later construction, are debated (Cornell, Beginnings of Rome).

events.title: Anti-Pythagorean risings in Magna Graecia
events.summary: Around the mid-5th century popular risings destroyed the Pythagorean political clubs that dominated Croton and other Italiote cities; the meeting house in Croton was burned with its members inside, and survivors such as Philolaus fled to Greece.
events.detail: Polybius says the burning of the Pythagorean synedria throughout Magna Graecia brought chaos until the Achaeans of the Peloponnese mediated and the cities adopted Achaean institutions. Later the Pythagorean Archytas governed Tarentum (c. 367-347). The episode shows how philosophical brotherhoods acted as oligarchic parties in the Greek West.
events.debate: Date (c. 510, c. 450 or several waves) disputed.

events.title: Murder of Lucius Siccius Dentatus
events.summary: L. Siccius Dentatus, the plebeian 'Roman Achilles' with 45 wounds in front, eight single combats and 14 civic crowns, was sent by the decemvirs to choose a campsite and murdered by the soldiers escorting him; his body was found among dead escorts with no enemy slain.
events.detail: Siccius had been urging the troops to secede. His record (120 battles, nine triumphs following generals) is preserved in Pliny, Dionysius and Gellius with variants; it is a later catalogue of military virtue but expresses the idea that plebeian valour carried the early Republic. The murder, with the Verginia affair, triggered the mutiny of the armies.

events.title: First triumph voted by the people against the Senate
events.summary: After L. Valerius defeated the Aequi and Volsci and M. Horatius the Sabines, the Senate refused them triumphs; the tribune L. Icilius carried a vote of the people granting both, the first triumph celebrated by popular decision without senatorial authority.
events.detail: The episode reinforces the image of Valerius and Horatius as the pro-plebeian consuls of the restoration. It became a precedent: in 356 C. Marcius Rutilus, the first plebeian dictator, and in 223 C. Flaminius triumphed by popular vote against the Senate.

events.title: Prosecution of the decemvirs
events.summary: Verginius, now tribune, prosecuted Appius Claudius, who appealed to the people under the provocatio he had denied others; imprisoned before trial, he killed himself, as did Sp. Oppius; the other decemvirs went into exile and their property was confiscated.
events.detail: M. Claudius, the client who had claimed Verginia as his slave, was condemned but allowed to go into exile at Tibur. The tribune M. Duillius then declared an end to prosecutions, a kind of amnesty. Livy's account builds the restoration of 449 as a constitutional reset, with the leges Valeriae Horatiae guaranteeing appeal and tribunician sacrosanctity.

events.title: Lex Trebonia on tribunician elections
events.summary: When only five tribunes were elected in 448 and they co-opted two patricians, the tribune L. Trebonius carried a law that the presiding tribune must continue the election until all ten places were filled by vote, outlawing co-optation.
events.detail: Co-optation had allowed patricians into the college. The law also shows the tribunate as an elected office of the concilium plebis, distinct from the magistracies of the whole people.

events.title: Aequian and Volscian raid to the Esquiline Gate
events.summary: Exploiting civil strife, the Aequi and Volsci raided up to the Esquiline Gate; T. Quinctius Capitolinus, consul for the fourth time, rallied the plebs with a famous speech and with Agrippa Furius defeated the invaders.
events.detail: Livy claims the booty was claimed by the Roman people in the notorious Ardea-Aricia arbitration of the same year. The episode illustrates how close the Aequian frontier still lay in the 440s.
events.locName: Between Rome and the Alban hills

battle.significance: Removed an immediate threat to Rome.

events.title: Panhellenic foundation of Thurii
events.summary: Athens organised a panhellenic colony near the site of Sybaris, led by Lampon and Xenocritus; Protagoras is said to have drafted its laws, Hippodamus of Miletus may have planned it on a grid, and Herodotus and the orator Lysias became citizens.
events.detail: The original Sybarite settlers claimed privileges and were expelled or killed. The citizens were organised in ten tribes by origin (Athenian, Arcadian, Achaean and others), and the city soon broke with Athens, Delphi declaring Apollo its founder. Thurii fought Tarentum over the Siritis, and its appeals to Rome against the Lucanians in the 280s helped draw Rome into southern Italy.

events.title: Treaty with Ardea and the linen books
events.summary: After the first consular tribunes abdicated as improperly elected, the suffect consuls L. Papirius Mugillanus and L. Sempronius Atratinus renewed the treaty with Ardea; Licinius Macer later found their names both in the treaty and in the 'linen books' (libri lintei) kept in the temple of Juno Moneta.
events.detail: Livy notes that the annals and the lists of magistrates omitted these consuls, which shows how Roman historians reconstructed the Fasti from documents. The libri lintei were magistrate lists on linen, consulted by Macer and Tubero in the 1st century BC; their authenticity was questioned already by Livy.
events.debate: Value of the libri lintei and the suffect consulship of 444 are disputed.

events.title: Formation of the Campanian people
events.summary: Diodorus notes under 438 that 'the nation of the Campanians was formed, named for the fertility of the plain': Oscan-speaking newcomers from the Samnite hills organised a federal people centred on Capua, a prelude to seizing Etruscan Capua (423) and Greek Cumae (421).
events.detail: The Campanians kept Oscan as their language and the meddix tuticus as chief magistrate. Their cavalry was famous and their mercenaries served in Sicily for Carthage and Dionysius, later seizing Entella, Aetna and Messana. The distinction between lowland Campanians and highland Samnites became the fault line of the First Samnite War.

events.title: Fidenae defects and murders Rome's envoys
events.summary: Fidenae, a Roman colony on the Tiber, defected to Lars Tolumnius of Veii and killed four Roman envoys, C. Fulcinius, Cloelius Tullus, Sp. Antius and L. Roscius, at Tolumnius' prompting; Rome set up their statues on the Rostra.
events.detail: Cicero and Pliny saw the statues, which stood until the late Republic and were among the oldest portrait statues in Rome. Killing envoys violated the ius gentium and justified the war in which A. Cornelius Cossus killed Tolumnius and won the spolia opima.

events.title: Plague and famine of 436-433
events.summary: Repeated pestilence afflicted Rome from 436; in 433 the Temple of Apollo Medicus was vowed 'for the health of the people', and grain was bought in Etruria, the Pomptine plain, Cumae and Sicily.
events.detail: Livy notes that the plague kept Rome from exploiting the destruction of Fidenae. The vow to Apollo, Rome's first Greek healing cult with its own temple, was fulfilled in 431 by the consul Cn. Julius.

events.title: Etruscan league refuses aid to Veii
events.summary: Veii and Falerii sent envoys to the council of the twelve Etruscan peoples at the sanctuary of Voltumna; the league refused to make their war its own, the first of several such refusals that left Veii isolated.
events.detail: The Fanum Voltumnae near Volsinii hosted annual assemblies, games and the election of a federal priest. Livy records later council meetings in 405, 403 and 389. Excavations at Campo della Fiera below Orvieto since 2000 have found a large sanctuary with temples, a sacred way and votives, now widely accepted as the Fanum.
scholarship: Stopponi, excavations at Campo della Fiera (2000-)

events.title: Lex Aemilia limits the censorship to 18 months
events.summary: The dictator Mam. Aemilius Mamercinus carried a law cutting the censors' tenure from five years to eighteen months; the censors in office took revenge by removing him from his tribe and rating him an aerarius taxed at eight times his assessment.
events.detail: The law fixed the shape of the censorship for the rest of the Republic: censors elected every five years (later) but holding office only eighteen months, long enough to complete the census and let contracts. Livy says the people were outraged by the censors' revenge; Mamercus reportedly bore it calmly.

events.title: Tarentum and Thurii found Heraclea
events.summary: After fighting over the Siritis, Tarentum and Thurii jointly founded Heraclea near the old Ionian colony of Siris; Tarentum soon dominated it, and it became the meeting place of the Italiote League.
events.detail: The Heraclea Tablets, bronze inscriptions of c. 300 recording temple land surveys, and the later Tabula Heracleensis with Roman municipal law were found nearby. Pyrrhus defeated the Romans on the Siris plain in 280; in 278 Heraclea obtained an unusually favourable treaty with Rome.

events.title: First law against electoral canvassing
events.summary: To stop patricians from using conspicuous canvassing against plebeian candidates for the consular tribunate, the tribunes carried a law forbidding candidates to whiten their togas with chalk.
events.detail: The word candidatus comes from the chalk-whitened toga (toga candida). Livy calls this the first law on ambitus; later ones followed in 358, 181, 159 and onward.

events.title: Postumius Tubertus and the execution of his son
events.summary: A story told that the dictator A. Postumius Tubertus, victor at Mount Algidus, had his son beheaded for leaving his post to fight, even though he won; Livy rejects it, but 'imperia Postumiana' became a proverb for pitiless discipline.
events.detail: Livy argues that the proverb belongs to Manlius Torquatus (340), whose execution of his son was certain, and doubts the Postumian version for lack of evidence. The doublet shows how family traditions competed for famous exempla.

events.title: Leontini's appeal and the first Athenian intervention in Sicily
events.summary: Leontini, at war with Syracuse, sent the orator Gorgias to Athens, which dispatched Laches with twenty ships in 427; the Congress of Gela (424), where Hermocrates urged 'Sicily for the Sicilians', ended the war.
events.detail: Gorgias' speeches at Athens introduced Sicilian rhetoric to the city. Athens' motive, according to Thucydides, was to stop Sicilian grain reaching the Peloponnese and to test the conquest of the island. The intervention set the precedent for the great expedition of 415.

events.title: Sextus Tempanius saves the army against the Volsci
events.summary: When the consul C. Sempronius Atratinus' army was being beaten by the Volsci, the cavalry decurion Sextus Tempanius had his troopers dismount and fight on foot, restoring the line; both armies withdrew believing themselves defeated.
events.detail: Tempanius was honoured by the plebs and elected tribune; Sempronius was prosecuted and in 420 fined 15,000 asses. The story illustrates the early cavalry's habit of dismounting, which Livy repeats elsewhere.

battle.significance: Indecisive; led to the prosecution of the consul.

events.title: Trial of the Vestal Postumia
events.summary: The Vestal Postumia was tried for unchastity because of her elegant dress and too-free wit; she was acquitted, and the pontifex maximus ordered her to abstain from jokes and to dress with more holiness than elegance.
events.detail: Livy's terse story is valuable because it shows suspicion of incestum resting on manner rather than evidence, and the pontifex maximus' disciplinary power over the Vestals.

events.title: Agrarian bill of Maecilius and Metilius
events.summary: The tribunes Sp. Maecilius and M. Metilius proposed that land taken from enemies be distributed man by man; the patricians defeated it by persuading other tribunes to veto, a tactic Livy credits to Ap. Claudius.
events.detail: The 'divide the tribunes' tactic became a standard patrician defence and foreshadows the deposition of Octavius by Ti. Gracchus in 133.
